summary: Active measurements over the public Internet sometimes hit parties who didn't agree to them and may see them as aggressive. This document suggests simple techniques for a probe source to identify itself, explaining what the probe is, its purpose, and who to contact. It relies on offline analysis and needs no changes to the data or control plane.

eli5.summary: If a stranger knocks on your door, you'd like a note saying who they are and why. This says how internet test packets can carry a note like that.

subtitle: Simple techniques for identifying who sent measurement probes across the Internet.

tldr.problem: Researchers send test packets (probes) across the Internet to study network topology and performance, but recipients who receive these unsolicited probes do not know who sent them, why, or how to contact the source. This can trigger security alerts and requires manual investigation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes two techniques: an out-of-band method where the probe's source IP address points to a web page describing the measurement, and an in-band method where the probe packet itself carries contact information embedded in its payload or extension headers.
tldr.outcome: Recipients of research probes can quickly understand their purpose and contact the researchers, reducing unnecessary alarm and facilitating ethical measurement research.

today: RFC 9511 is an Informational RFC published in November 2023. The RFC does not mandate any action but provides guidance for researchers and network operators. The well-known URI "probing.txt" has been registered with IANA. Adoption depends on voluntary implementation by measurement researchers and infrastructure operators willing to publish or read probe attribution information.

sections.title: Why Probes Need Attribution
sections.content:
Network researchers perform active measurements by sending test packets to study Internet topology and performance. But when an organization receives an unsolicited probe from an unknown source, it looks like a potential attack. The recipients must then investigate offline using packet captures to understand what happened.

This document provides simple techniques to help recipients identify what the probe is, its purpose, and whom to contact. The methods require no changes to the Internet's core data or control planes, and they rely on offline analysis so the measurement itself is not disrupted.
sections.eli5: When someone sends you a test packet, you'd like to know who sent it and why. These techniques let researchers include a note with their contact information.

sections.title: Out-of-Band Attribution: Reverse DNS Lookup
sections.content:
The first method uses reverse DNS. When a recipient receives a probe from an IP address, they can reverse-resolve that address to a domain name, then visit a special web page at /.well-known/probing.txt on that domain. This file describes what probes from that source are being sent, their purpose, and contact information.

For example, if a probe comes from IP address 2001:db8:dead::1, and reverse DNS resolves it to example.net, the recipient can access https://example.net/.well-known/probing.txt to find information. If reverse DNS fails, the recipient can try accessing a URL based on the IP address itself, like https://[2001:db8:dead::1]/.well-known/probing.txt. The Probe Description File must follow a standard format defined in RFC 9116, including fields like Contact, Expires, and a Description of the measurement being performed.
sections.eli5: Like reading the return address on an envelope. You look up where the probe came from and visit a website explaining what the researcher is doing.

sections.title: In-Band Attribution: Embedding Contact Information in Probes
sections.content:
The second method includes contact information directly in the probe packet itself. For ICMP echo requests, the URI can be placed in the data field. For UDP or TCP packets, it goes in the payload. For IPv6 packets, it can be embedded in a special option inside a Hop-by-Hop or Destination Options extension header.

The URI must be null-terminated and can point to a web page (https://example.net/measurement.txt), an email address (mailto:lab@example.net), or a phone number (tel:+1-201-555-0123). The advantage is that the information travels with the probe itself, so recipients do not need to do a reverse DNS lookup. The disadvantage is that adding data to the probe packet might change how intermediate routers or endpoints handle it, potentially biasing the measurement or causing the probe to be dropped.
sections.eli5: Like writing your phone number inside the envelope. The note travels with the packet so the recipient doesn't have to look anything up.

sections.title: Ethical and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is designed to support ethical researchers who want to conduct measurements responsibly. However, the techniques themselves are simple and could be used maliciously to spoof the identity of the true probe source. Recipients cannot trust the attribution information without independent verification, such as confirming that the domain matches the reverse DNS or checking other indicators.

The out-of-band method has the advantage that it does not affect the probe packet itself, so measurements are not biased. The in-band method covers cases where the source IP address is not owned by the researcher (such as RIPE Atlas probes sent from a vantage point), or when dynamic addressing makes out-of-band lookup impossible. Using both methods together provides the strongest attribution signal, as recipients can cross-check the web page with information embedded in the packet.
sections.eli5: Bad actors could fake the note, so you should still verify before trusting. But for honest researchers, this helps everyone understand what's happening.
